description:
Ash Watch tells a water manager, days after a wildfire, which drinking-water sources sit below badly burned steep slopes, and how much rain will wash the ash in. 

The fire is out. The danger isn't.

We're a team of a mathematician Andrea and BI analyst Maria.
summary:
Ash Watch is a post-fire warning for drinking water, built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. After a wildfire, the first heavy rain washes ash, sediment and metals into the streams, reservoirs and wells that towns drink from. Ash Watch tells every town and reservoir downstream how its water could be polluted, through which of four pathways (surface runoff, debris flow, groundwater, airborne ash), at how much rain, and how confident each estimate is.
 
NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar is at the core: its HV channel measures the woody fuel before the fire, confirms the burn through smoke and cloud, and tracks regrowth every 12 days. We fuse it with Sentinel-2, terrain, soil, wind and NASA GPM rainfall, and show the result on a scrolling story map.
 
Demo: the Burgohondo fire in Ávila, Spain (July 2026). Using only data up to 25 September, Ash Watch rated Piedralaves and Casavieja high: the two towns whose tap water was declared unfit after the October rain. Every input is global and open, so the pipeline can be re-run for another fire.
details:
What it does

After a wildfire, the danger to drinking water starts when the fire ends. In October 2026, the first autumn rain washed ash from the Burgohondo fire into the rivers of Ávila, and tap water in Casavieja and Piedralaves was declared unfit to drink, two months after the fire was under control.

For every town and reservoir downstream of a fire, Ash Watch gives one card:

- a level (high, medium, low) for four pollution pathways: surface runoff (rain washing ash into streams and reservoirs), debris flow (a short, intense storm sending mud and ash into intakes), groundwater (which wells and springs to test first) and airborne ash (ash that fell on a reservoir during the fire);

- the evidence behind each level and a confidence label: high for runoff, medium for debris flow, screening for groundwater, indicative for airborne ash;

- the rain intensity that would trigger a debris flow;

- a radar recovery series showing whether vegetation is coming back;

- the first lab tests to run: turbidity, manganese, zinc, lead, nitrate, phosphorus, dissolved organic carbon.

How it works

A 13-step Python pipeline runs once per fire and exports a few small files that a static story site reads.

- Radar. Every NISAR L2 GCOV acquisition is cut to the area: four passes, June to November 2026. HH and HV backscatter before and after the fire are compared within the same pass, so the viewing geometry is identical. HV comes from branches and trunks, so it measures woody biomass and drops where the forest burned. HH responds to bare, wet ground.

- Burn and severity. A pixel counts as burned where the radar HV drop and the Sentinel-2 burn index (dNBR) agree; under cloud or smoke the radar decides alone. Inside the burn, Sentinel-2 grades severity, and a random forest trained on the radar fills the class where the ground was hidden.

- Fuel and ash. Pre-fire HV is calibrated against ESA CCI Biomass to map fuel. Fuel times the share burned times the ash fraction gives the ash load. The fractions are known only as ranges from the literature, so a Monte Carlo of 5,000 draws gives a P10 to P90 range.

- Water. Flow routing on the Copernicus 30 m terrain model links every hillside to the stream and town below it. A sediment delivery ratio gives the ash that reaches each town. The published USGS debris-flow model (Staley et al. 2017) gives each small stream a likelihood and a rain trigger.

- Screening layers. A simplified DRASTIC index scores 449 mapped wells and springs, and ERA5 wind during the fire gives a downwind exposure index.

- Check. NASA GPM IMERG rainfall from the October storm is compared with each town's trigger.

Results for Ávila

- From data ending 25 September, before the first rain on 3 October, Piedralaves, Casavieja and both reservoirs (El Burguillo and San Juan) are rated high. 75 places were rated: 7 high, 3 medium, 65 low.

- Ash load: about 30,000 t (P10 15,500 t, P90 48,000 t). Lowest debris-flow trigger: 13.3 mm/h, above El Burguillo reservoir.

- On 6 November, radar HV over the burned land upstream of Piedralaves and Casavieja was still 4 to 5 dB below its pre-fire level: no woody regrowth yet.

- Compared with the official EU burned-area map (EFFIS, 62,372 ha), 93% of what we map as burned is inside the official perimeter, but we find only about a quarter of it. Our rule requires radar and optical data to agree, and where shrubs and understory burned the radar saw too little change. So ash, burned share and debris-flow likelihood are lower bounds: with a fuller burn map, levels can only go up. Piedralaves and Casavieja, 84% and 96% inside the official perimeter, are rated high even so.

Benefits

- A ranked list of towns could be ready within weeks of the fire, before the first heavy rain, while utilities can still prepare backup supply, protect intakes and test wells.

- Each card explains why it says what it says and how sure it is, in plain language.

- Radar works through smoke and cloud, and NISAR revisits every 12 days, so the assessment can follow the recovery.

- It uses only free, open data and open-source code, so a small municipality or utility can use it without a licence or a field campaign.

Intended impact

Pollution after a fire lasts for years: across 500 western-US watersheds, pollutants peaked at up to 103 times pre-fire levels, with nitrogen and sediment high for up to eight years. In the United States, the USGS publishes post-fire debris-flow assessments within days, and WEPPcloud models ash and sediment for individual water-supply catchments. In Europe, EFFIS and Copernicus map the burn but stop there, and post-fire protection of drinking water is decided case by case. Ash Watch aims to give town halls, water utilities, river basin authorities and civil protection a fast first screening of every town at risk, so detailed models and field crews go where they are needed first.

How it is creative

- Following the ash all the way to the tap. Most fire products stop at "where did it burn". Ash Watch follows the ash downhill to each town's water and turns it into a rain threshold and a test list a mayor can act on.

- One radar across the whole timeline. The same NISAR HV channel gives the fuel before the fire, confirms the burn where smoke hides the ground, and tracks regrowth afterwards. As far as we found, none of the operational post-fire tools uses radar.

- Four pathways, four confidence labels. Runoff, debris flow, groundwater and airborne ash appear side by side, each labelled with how much the evidence supports it, instead of one blended score.

- Uncertainty carried to the user. The ash range on each card comes from a Monte Carlo of the uncertain combustion and ash fractions.

- Story as data. The site's narrative lives in a data file, so a new fire needs new data and new text, not new code.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

- Pipeline: Python (rasterio, h5py, xarray, pysheds, scikit-learn, geopandas, asf_search, earthaccess, cdsapi).

- Story site: Vite, React and MapLibre GL JS; static files only, deployed to GitHub Pages by GitHub Actions.

- Quality: a data-contract checker runs in CI on every pull request; a synthetic end-to-end test runs the whole chain on fake data in minutes.

- Hardware: one Linux machine with 16 cores and 64 GB of memory; processing took under an hour. The main cost is downloading 70 to 80 GB of NISAR files; a pass-by-pass mode needs about 30 GB of disk. No custom hardware.

- Data: NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV (ASF DAAC), NASA GPM IMERG, Copernicus Sentinel-2 and DEM GLO-30, ESA CCI Biomass, ERA5, ISRIC SoilGrids, OpenStreetMap; EFFIS burnt areas for an independent comparison.

- Licence: Apache-2.0.

What we considered

- Honesty over impressiveness. One fire is a case study, not a validation. The debris-flow model was calibrated in the western United States, so we use it as a ranking. Groundwater and airborne ash are labelled screening and indicative and never drive a town's overall level.

- Checking against independent data. We compared our burned area with the official EFFIS map and report both precision (93%) and recall (24%). Our ash and risk numbers are presented as lower bounds.

- What the hindcast can and cannot show. Satellite rain (IMERG, 10 km, 30-minute averages) never passed any town's debris-flow trigger. It smooths out the short bursts that trigger debris flows, so it can neither confirm nor reject a trigger. What happened in October, black water and unfit tap water, is the runoff pathway, which needs no 15-minute trigger. We show the result rather than hide it.

- Users. One card per town, plain language, and an action list (which tests, which wells).

- Reproducibility. Every unmeasured number is marked as an assumption in one configuration file; nothing is hard-coded.

- Ethics and copyright. We link to news reports and never reuse their photos. We used AI assistance.

Re-using Ash Watch for another fire or region

What carries over unchanged

- The code. A new fire is a new configuration file: bounding box, map projection, fire dates, the before and after windows, and the towns and reservoirs to name. The steps, the data contract and the site code stay the same.

- The data. Every input has a global open version: NISAR covers all land every 12 days; Sentinel-2, the Copernicus DEM, ESA CCI Biomass, SoilGrids, ERA5, IMERG and OpenStreetMap are global; EFFIS (Europe) or GWIS (worldwide) provide an official perimeter.

- The cost. One machine, under an hour of processing; most of the time goes to downloading the radar files.

What must be checked or changed for each new fire

- Burn rule. Our radar-and-optical rule found only a quarter of the Ávila fire, because shrub and understory burns barely change HV. For shrubland or grassland fires this will be worse. Before re-use, the rule should accept a moderate Sentinel-2 burn without a radar drop, and use the EFFIS or GWIS perimeter as the outer limit; the pipeline already reads a perimeter file. This fix is planned, not done.

- Timing windows. The post-fire window must end before the rainy season (or snow), or wet soil confuses the radar. In wet or snowy climates there may be no clean window.

- Data availability. Calibrated NISAR products exist only for acquisitions since 17 June 2026, with a data gap from 27 July to 10 August 2026; reprocessing of earlier data is planned for 2027. Fires before mid-2026 cannot use NISAR yet.

- Fuel and ash. The biomass calibration is re-fitted automatically on each run, but L-band HV saturates near 100 Mg/ha, so dense temperate or tropical forest gives a lower bound. The ash fractions come from the literature and fit forests like Ávila's; peat, eucalypt or boreal fires need different ranges in the configuration file.

- Debris-flow model. It is calibrated in the western US. Elsewhere it gives a ranking, not a probability, until it is re-fitted on a local inventory of debris flows.

- Where water comes from. Towns are linked to the stream they sit on, using OpenStreetMap. Many towns take water from a reservoir or network elsewhere: El Barraco, in the news, is rated low because its own catchment did not burn. Real use needs the utilities' intake locations.

- Groundwater. The default uses a terrain proxy and uniform aquifer ratings. Karst regions, common around the Mediterranean, need local hydrogeology; the pipeline already accepts global water-table depth (Fan et al.) and permeability (GLHYMPS) layers.

- Rain check. IMERG is too coarse for 15-minute triggers. Where national weather-radar rainfall or gauges exist, they should replace it.

- Story. The site's text and camera positions are written for Ávila and need rewriting; the town cards and the map work as they are.
